title: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna
hook: "take care." "love, Mom." a sign-off said over and over can still mean everything. hymns in the Rig Veda's seventh book share one
carry: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna, called in pairs: Mitra and Varuna, Indra and Agni, joined in one word.

Take care. Drive safe. Love, Mom. Text me when you get home. Some goodbyes get said so often they're worn smooth, like a step everyone uses. And still, if the person who always says drive safe forgets one day, it's noticed. A sign-off that sounds routine can carry a whole relationship. The Rig Veda has one. In its seventh book, the hymns credited to the seer Vasishtha's family, one closing line returns at the end of hymn after hymn: to Agni, to Indra, to Ushas, to Varuna. Today, the last day on these hymns: how they say goodbye.
screen: `TAKE CARE. DRIVE SAFE. LOVE, MOM.` → `WORN SMOOTH, STILL MEANT.` → `HOW THE HYMNS SAY GOODBYE.`

segments.voice: The line is yuyam pata svastibhih sada nah. In plain English: you, protect us always with blessings. Svasti is well-being, things going well. Pata means protect, keep. Sada, always. Nah, us. Now listen to the first word. Yuyam is you, but plural: you all. Even when a hymn has spent its whole length praising one god, the dawn, say, or the fire, the last line can turn and speak to the gods together. Thank you, Agni, for this morning, and all of you: keep us well. The hymn to Varuna from two days ago, where the singer asks what he did wrong, closes this way too. After all that worry, the ending is the same steady line as the hymns of praise. Whatever happened in the middle, the sign-off doesn't change. A refrain isn't lazy writing. It's a promise of return. The singer says it at the end of the dawn hymn and again at the end of the fire hymn, and the repeating is part of the meaning: keep us well, always, the way we keep coming back. And notice what's asked for. Not victory, not riches. Just svasti, well-being, kept. Each of the four voices has had its day. This is how their hymns close: one ordinary, enormous wish, said to all of them at once.
screen: `YUYAM PATA SVASTIBHIH SADA NAH.` · `YUYAM: YOU, PLURAL. ALL OF YOU.` · `THE SAME LINE, AFTER PRAISE OR WORRY.` · `SVASTI: WELL-BEING, KEPT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you'll see or talk to today, one face at a time, and with each out-breath wish them one plain thing: be well. Then widen it the way yuyam does, to all of them together, the people they love, and the ones you won't meet. If you pray, pray for them in your own words.
Hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. Today, the closing line of hymns in the seventh book: you all, protect us always with well-being. Today's word.
Your line: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. Keep us well, all of you, always. Four voices, heard.

original.note: Sanskrit: well-being, things going well. In the closing line of hymns in Rig Veda book seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn ends where its praise ends.
what it means: hymns in book seven close with one shared line, turned to all the gods: protect us always with well-being.
what a scholar hears: yūyaṃ pāta svastibhiḥ sadā naḥ, the Vasiṣṭha refrain; yūyam is second-person plural, so even a hymn to one god ends by addressing many.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home

chat.says: Why does that closing line say 'you all' if the hymn praised one god?
options: Yuyam is plural: the last line turns to the gods together and asks, keep us well.
It's a copying slip; the line was meant to name only the hymn's own god.
It speaks to the people listening, asking them to protect the singer.
chat.meaning: Yuyam means you all: the book-seven refrain turns to the gods together with one wish, protect us always with well-being.

Vasishtha.meaning: a seer; book seven is credited to his family

Varuna.meaning: the god who keeps rita, the world's order
